A Better Picture

By morning, Dutch had painted Tahiti over the only chart with the inlet's depth markings.

Brian found him at the mess table, adding a happy little tree to the place where the launch had sunk.

“That was a shoal.”

“It was an ugly shoal.”

“It still is.”

“Not in here.”

Dutch tapped the side of his head, winced, and moved the finger to the paper.

Dr. Evil stopped behind him.

“I see the head injury has acquired a studio.”

Dutch placed a thumb over the sea wall.

“Everybody keeps telling us what we can't do. Can't go through there. Can't get the last case. Can't make an island.”

“The first two have supporting evidence.”

Brian consulted a page beneath the table.

“What matters is we're following your plan.”

Dutch looked at him.

“Why?”

Brian blinked.

“Because you're the leader.”

“Is that a reason to follow a bad plan?”

“No.”

“Then tell me why it's good.”

The little man had bought a walkthrough for a man who had changed his fucking settings.

“We should get Merrit,” he said.

Dutch laid down the brush.

“Look at you. First man with a clipboard in a garden.”

Brian looked at the painting, then down at the page beneath the table.

Dutch leaned across and caught its edge.

Brian held on.

“What is that?”

“Personal preparation.”

“About me.”

“Leadership research.”

Dutch tugged.

The damp sheet tore.

He lifted his half. Brian kept the other.

Under the word LOYALTY, the crew researcher had written: does not experience public correction as neutral.

Dutch read it aloud.

Then he looked around the mess compartment.

Brian had chosen an extraordinarily bad room in which to ask whether they could do this privately.

Dr. Evil put his cup down.

“Those are my discarded notes.”

Brian looked at him.

“I was going to organize—”

“You organized yourself onto them.”

Dutch turned the half page over.

“Does it say what I do now?”

Brian's eyes went involuntarily to the other half.

Clifford, arriving in the doorway, saw it.

“Whatever it says, don't.”

Dutch started to laugh.

It was not the laugh Brian had planned to receive. It rose, stopped against the pain in his head, then returned louder.

“You've got a little book of me.”

“It's not little.”

“Stand up and show me, then.”

Brian stayed on the chair.

Dutch held the torn page beside Bob Ross's portrait.

“Bob, you hearing this? We got a boy who thinks he can read the weather.”

The cheek did not answer.

Dutch waited half a beat, nodded anyway and went back to the sky.

“You want to know what I do next? So do I. That's the adventure.”

He painted a yellow sun directly over the point where the channel forked.

Brian folded his half of the page so tightly it would no longer lie flat.

Merrit arrived with a piece of bread, escorted by a crewman. He had spent the night in a utility compartment with somebody outside the door. He looked at the painting and made the reasonable calculation that he would like to leave alive.

“Very fine.”

Dutch turned the picture toward him.

“Where does it put you in mind of?”

“A warm place.”

“Tahiti.”

“Just like it.”

“You've been?”

“No.”

“Then you can imagine.”

“Yes.”

“Good. Show us the way in.”

Merrit looked at the painted beach.

“That used to be the mud.”

“Not anymore.”

“It'll be mud when we get there.”

Clifford folded his arms.

“I thought we were leaving.”

“We are,” Dutch said. “After we finish.”

“Yesterday you said finishing meant leaving.”

“Then we've made progress.”

Merrit described the maintenance ledge beneath the store. A signal tower watched the approach. Dutch found its little inked shape sticking through his sunset.

“That ruins it.”

“The approach?” Brian asked.

“The composition.”

Dr. Evil handed Merrit a piece of packing paper.

“Draw something that floats.”

Harl's extra watch had collected around the burned exhibition court. Tai Lung had left after taking the champion's belt directly from Harl and refusing to wear the sash. Nobody on the submarine knew where he had gone.

The smaller store still had two men at its stair.

Merrit led the thieves along the exposed low-tide ledge. Dr. Evil promised him release when the last case came out. Merrit made him say it plainly.

Then he went around the bend and called that the robbers were below.

One guard leaned over the stair rail. Clifford struck the rifle upward. Its shot broke brick above them. Dutch fired past his shoulder; the guard fell. Clifford clubbed the other man behind the ear and took his keys.

Merrit opened the store.

Up in the tower, a signalman reached for the red flag.

Brian saw him through borrowed field glasses.

“Flag!”

Clifford got behind the net floats as a pistol shot splintered the rail beside his hand.

Dutch stared at the tower.

“Take it down.”

“The bell rope?” Clifford asked.

“The ugly son of a bitch holding it!”

Dutch was unfolding his painting under fire.

There are men who die for art. Dutch appeared determined to start with somebody else's employees.

Clifford cut the bell rope with the saber. The flag was already up. Across the basin a patrol boat turned toward the pier.

At the near tower foot, old water damage had opened the wood around its bolts. Two diagonal braces kept it upright.

Dutch pointed with the rolled painting.

“There!”

Clifford followed the actual load, not the brush. He cut the exposed iron eye securing the brace nearest the water and backed away as the released timber whipped across the pier.

The rotten foot split.

“Off the stair!” Clifford shouted.

Dutch stayed to admire the lean.

“Dutch!”

He moved.

The tower came down across the patrol entrance. Its upper platform broke against the sea wall; the red flag went under. The signalman jumped, caught a crosspiece and hung above the water while his own men threw him a line.

Merrit and Dr. Evil emerged with the last case.

“Look,” Dutch said, pointing at the open sky. “Now it breathes.”

Clifford grabbed the case's free handle.

The thieves went down the ledge, boarded their waiting service boat and left the patrol dealing with a landscape improvement.

Merrit stayed on the slip.

The doctor looked back.

“Your consultancy has concluded.”

Merrit ran.

Dutch held his painting beside the real coast on the ride home. Every missing piece of tower proved him more correct.

By afternoon, Sella had all four instruments. She paid the remaining hundred and thirty after the thirty-silver launch deduction. Dr. Evil paid Arthur the promised thirty for the spirits. TPP had a hundred and sixty-six left. With Daynah's eight added, the Sins' common purse held two thousand four hundred and ninety-one.

Dutch tried to give Sella the painting instead of a receipt.

She stepped around it.

He watched her go.

“No vision,” he said.

Brian returned the field glasses.

Dr. Evil stopped him with a hand on the case.

“You called the flag. You didn't guess.”

“I didn't know about the brace.”

“That wasn't your job.”

Brian looked at the doctor.

“The announcement equipment,” Dr. Evil continued. “After you've rested. We can make a space for your work.”

Brian nodded.

He carried that sentence back to his berth as carefully as the wet research.

Shake sat in Brian's chair, reading the lyric page Brian had left with him after boarding the previous afternoon.

“That's private.”

“You gave me this page yesterday. I asked if I could look, remember?”

Brian stopped.

Shake held up the sheet Brian had left with him the previous night.

“Oh. That.”

“I like it.”

“People don't always get the layers.”

“I get enough. Can I try it?”

“Try what?”

“Rapping it.”

Brian sat on the bunk.

“It's not really written for your cadence.”

“What cadence do I have?”

Brian opened his mouth.

Shake waited.

“It's character-led,” Brian said.

“Great. I am one.”

Shake tapped the edge of the chair with his straw.

Not randomly. A clean little click, a space, two quick taps. He made the empty berth sound as though somebody had finally put a drummer in it.

He started with Brian's pipeline line.

He didn't improve the words yet. He changed where they landed.

The first pressure came late, dragging behind the taps. The second hit early. Pipeline broke across the beat and joined the next line instead of sitting there waiting to be congratulated.

Brian's fingers moved against his knee.

Shake caught the motion and gave him space for it.

“Yeah,” Brian said, before he could stop himself.

Shake left the page on the chair.

He kept going.

“Got a room full of noise and a fist full of wire,
everybody say it's dead till I put it through the fire.
Run a line through the wall, let the whole damn block hear,
you can bury what I built, can't bury what I brought here.

Took my name off the door, still my hand on the hinge,
little room, big sound, let the whole ship cringe.
If they paid for the quiet, put the price on the beat,
now the hush got a budget and the budget got feet.”

He shifted the tapping to the chair's metal edge.

The sound sharpened.

“Who put the wire through the wall? Who made the picture hold?
who got the whole damn room to laugh when the mighty got exposed?
Don't need another body's name to tell me what I made,
put the credit where the work is, put the work above the grade.”

Brian nodded hard.

That was him. His editing. His real win.

Shake pointed with the straw on the next beat, not mocking him—giving him the line.

Brian came in late.

“Exactly, because the edit was—”

Shake caught the interruption, bent the rhythm around it and handed it back without making him look worse.

Brian laughed again.

Then he realized Shake had rescued his timing too.

Shake never looked pleased with himself about that part.

He dropped the tapping entirely after grade.

The silence landed where a snare should have been.

Brian clapped.

Twice, hard.

Shake leaned back into the rhythm, found the opening on Brian's knee and used it.

The next run tightened. He took an ugly phrase Brian had crossed out, split it over two bars, and turned its awkward pause into a delayed rhyme so clean that Brian laughed out loud.

“There!” Brian said. “That—”

Shake nodded.

“I know.”

He finished on the same two taps he had started with.

No insult hidden in it. No crowd waiting outside. A fucking milkshake had taken Brian's writing seriously and made it sound worth somebody's time.

Brian was still smiling when the thought arrived.

He stopped clapping.

Shake looked at the page.

“We could do something with that.”

“With my writing.”

“Yeah. You do the words. I do some of the delivery. You know recording stuff.”

Brian rubbed the palms he had just used to applaud.

“I don't need a frontman.”

“Then stand in front.”

“That's a very easy thing for you to say.”

Shake looked down at his cup.

“Not really.”

Brian's face tightened.

“You know exactly what I'm saying.”

“I thought you wanted people to hear it.”

“They need to hear me.”

“Then record yourself.”

“I have.”

Shake waited.

The truth had arrived and Brian needed it out of the room.

“There's a difference between a polished studio performance and somebody coming in here doing a party trick.”

“Then let's do it in a studio.”

“You don't get to solve every objection I have.”

Shake's straw stopped moving.

Brian heard himself.

He corrected the wrong part.

“Because it's not an objection. It's a boundary.”

Shake picked the page up and held it toward him.

Brian wouldn't take it yet.

He had to make refusing the offered thing look like the offered thing had failed.

“This is what happens,” he said. “You invite somebody into your process. Next thing, you're standing off to the side while everybody congratulates them on your work.”

“There isn't anybody here.”

“I know how people are.”

“You just clapped.”

“That was professional courtesy.”

Shake glanced at Brian's reddened palms.

“Looked pretty enthusiastic.”

Brian put both hands behind his back.

“The delivery is part of the writing.”

Shake looked up.

“Then write how I did it.”

Brian looked up.

Shake was not smirking.

That made it worse.

“You think I can't?”

“I think you can write. I said I liked it.”

“Before you changed it.”

“I didn't change that first part.”

“The implication was obvious.”

Shake looked around the empty berth.

“To who?”

Brian climbed off the bunk.

“I'm not having a public argument.”

“It ain't public.”

“I won't be humiliated in my own office.”

Shake glanced at the bed.

“Your pillow's got a sock on it.”

Brian snatched the sock away.

“That's acoustic treatment.”

Shake stared.

Then, for once in his life, he let an easy insult pass.

“Look. I was trying to make music with you.”

Brian turned toward the door.

“Permission to review a work isn't permission to assume its creator needs replacing.”

Shake picked up the page.

“Fine. Keep it.”

Brian took it.

Shake took a little scrap from the journal's loose sheets and wrote across it with Brian's pencil.

Good words. We should make something.

He put it on the bunk.

“I'm getting a drink.”

Brian stood aside to let him leave.

He waited until the steps were gone.

Then he tried the first line the way Shake had delivered it.

It didn't land.

He tried again, softer.

The pause came too early. He filled it with a cough and looked at the door as though somebody had done that to him.

On shore, Clifford had left the saber in his submarine berth and come to Billy with empty hands.

Chris was inside beside the original console. Billy took Jack in, showed him to the table and stayed exterior.

Chris pointed to the disabled custom cliff trigger.

“That one's off. Here's the return.”

He demonstrated it, then handed over the headset.

Jack tested the control himself.

The menu came up.

He loaded the fishing.

Meatwad settled a respectful distance from the little viewing screen.

“Can I watch?”

Jack nodded.

He put the headset on.

Water moved around a stone. Leaves shook above him. The virtual Uncle Arthur waited with a fishing rod.

Jack looked behind himself.

Grass. Trees. The path back.

He made his first cast too close to the bank. The line caught.

He froze.

Virtual Arthur crouched beside it.

“We can get that loose.”

No audience. No disgust. No lesson about how stupid Jack was for trying.

The hook came free.

Jack took the rod back.

His next cast went farther.

Outside, the actual Arthur watched Billy's quiet face.

“He settle?”

Chris answered through the banjo.

“He's fishing.”

Arthur nodded.

For a moment he looked as though he wanted to ask whether that meant anything about him.

He didn't.

Back aboard the submarine, Brian found Clifford's berth empty.

The saber lay on the shelf beside a folded coat.

He had seen it used. He had seen where the activation control sat. He checked the corridor, stepped onto the bottom bunk frame and lifted it down.

The hilt was heavier than his journal.

He wrapped it in his shirt and carried it against his chest.

At the berth door he stopped.

The ship's announcement speaker clicked. A crewman was testing the faulty circuit Dr. Evil wanted Brian to inspect. Half a sentence broke into static.

Brian looked toward the sound.

He could have gone to the workbench. He knew the fault pattern. He had been asked.

The wrapped hilt pressed against his ribs.

From the galley came Shake's voice, humming the hook he had just made.

Not loudly. Not for Brian.

The note came easily.

Brian's mouth opened with the same phrase, failed to find the first interval and closed.

He took one step toward the workbench.

Then he turned the other way.

By the galley door, he unfolded the shirt.

For a moment his fingers could not find the activation switch. He rotated the hilt until he recognized it, took a grip short enough not to strike the frame and waited until the corridor behind him cleared.

Nothing rushed him.

Nothing attacked him.

He went in anyway.

At the galley entrance he heard water running.

Shake stood alone beside the sink.

He turned.

“Hey. You think about—”

Brian activated the saber.

The red blade filled the doorway.

Shake looked from it to Brian.

“That's Clifford's.”

Brian stepped inside.

“Not every collaboration is healthy.”

Shake backed into the counter.

“Put that fucking thing down.”

“I offered access to my art. You tried to take ownership of my identity.”

“I offered to rap.”

“I heard what you offered.”

Shake reached for the pan beside the sink.

Brian swept the blade across his arm before he got it.

The arm dropped. The pan rang against the floor.

Shake screamed.

Brian had space to stop.

He looked directly at Shake.

Then he drove the saber through the center of his cup.

The blade burned through the smiling printed face and struck the counter behind him. The smell changed from hot paper to scorched sweetness.

Shake's remaining hand caught Brian's wrist.

For a second the milkshake held on.

Brian jerked free, drew the blade across and cut him open.

His body fell against the cabinet. Thick pale filling ran between the doors and spread over the floor.

The hand stopped moving.

Brian extinguished the saber.

He stood listening.

The tap kept running.

There was no beat in it. Nothing new had entered his head.

He tried to hum Shake's opening. The same ugly note came out.

He stepped around the spreading spill, wrapped the hilt again and left.

In his berth, the encouraging note lay beside his journal.

Brian picked it up.

He tore one corner.

Stopped.

Read it.

Good words.

He put the note between two blank pages reserved for new material and shut the cover.

The research went into his bag. So did the folded Busta Rhymes poster, his ordinary possessions and the stolen saber.

He wrote one sentence before leaving.

Departed leadership position to pursue direct-action personal development.

He underlined leadership.

Below it, he began a second sentence.

Established independent artistic direction following—

He stopped.

The paper beside his elbow still said Good words.

Brian covered it with the research.

Following inappropriate—

He scratched that out too. It sounded as though something had happened to him that would require questions.

He started a new line.

Taking back my power.

That looked better.

He read it aloud, tested how it sounded and nodded.

The saber lay beside the journal. Its blade was off. The tiny room looked exactly the same as it had before he brought it in.

Brian tried Shake's opening once more.

He still couldn't do it.

He shut the book hard enough to trap the tip of his pencil and break it.

That gave him something small, immediate and defensible to be angry about.

“Fucking cheap.”

He packed the broken pencil too.

At the gangplank, a crewman asked where he was going.

“Independent consultation.”

Brian went down before there was another question.

A coaster was loading farther along the quay. Earlier that day, its pilot had complained to Dutch about a black-armored stranger buying passage south after questioning traders about unfamiliar salvage. Brian had listened. Now he followed that lead.

Behind him, the ship's cook entered the galley.

The first shout brought two men down the corridor.

Nobody found a duel. They found a pan, a burning gouge in the counter, one severed arm and the rest of Shake where Brian had left him.

When Jack returned from fishing, he heard the news before reaching his berth.

His first fish had still been on the screen when he took the headset off.

He sat on his bunk.

Then he looked at the empty shelf.

He stood again.

Brian's berth was empty too.

Jack did not know everything. He knew enough to call for the crewman who had watched Brian leave.

Dr. Evil arrived carrying a small brass plate.

He had asked the engineer to make room on the announcement workbench.

BRIAN. PRODUCTION.

The plate stayed in his hand while Jack described the missing saber.

Down the corridor, a crewman asked whether to scrub the galley.

“No,” Jack said.

Dr. Evil lowered the plate.

For once, he did not correct who had given the order.

Before dark, Jack went back ashore. He told Arthur what had been found, what was missing and which crewman had seen Brian leave. He did not turn an empty berth into an eyewitness account of the killing.

Chris listened inside Billy through the exterior feed. Meatwad sat beside the returned headset. He asked once whether Shake was coming back.

Chris said no.

Meatwad put his little bowl away. Nobody told him to be funny.

Brian got across the water by repairing something before telling anybody what an expert he was.

It was a small but important departure.

The coaster's loudhailer had a loose return and a ruined connector. Brian found a compatible piece in its repair box, made the contact hold and tested it at low volume. The pilot canceled the fare he had demanded, gave Brian a berth among the covered supplies and told him not to perform through it.

Brian described that last condition as protection of unreleased material.

The coast slipped away. Days passed in the crossing and on the caravan road south of the landing. Northern Shurima was not Tatooine. Brian checked that with a trader twice, because the answer refused to become more helpful.

He worked for water and provisions, paid no fare from the Sins' money and kept the saber wrapped. At each supply stop, he asked about the black-armored traveler ahead of them.

At the desert-side salvage yard, he found him.

Starkiller stood beside a dismantled engine, inspecting a machine that could not take him anywhere he wanted to go.

Brian walked up with his journal beneath one arm and Clifford's stolen saber in both hands.

The armored head turned.

Brian activated the blade far enough away that he didn't cut his own book.

“Real.”

Starkiller looked at the hilt.

“Turn it off.”

Brian did.

“I've had practical experience.”

“With that?”

“Recent. Transformational. I'd like to discuss a mentorship opportunity.”

“Make it quick.”

The armored head was already turning away.

“Chris has an X-wing,” Brian blurted.

Starkiller stopped turning away.

Brian watched the change happen.

“Who?”

“A man I know. Personally. One of the Seven Sins. Not currently my organization, but legacy contacts remain.”

“Where is the ship?”

“I can give you context.”

“Give me a location.”

“Of course. But first I should explain what I bring to the table. Not physically. I'm aware of the table situation.”

Starkiller faced him fully.

Brian straightened.

“I know who you are. Vader trained you in secret. You fought him. They rebuilt you. It's honestly incredible what you've managed to accomplish under difficult supervision.”

“Where is the X-wing?”

“That's why this works. You need transport. I need advanced personal development. You trained under Vader; I train under you. We don't need the Emperor involved. I'm keeping the hierarchy lean.”

The masked face gave him nothing.

Brian took this as a listener waiting for the prepared portion.

He opened the journal.

“I've put the request into a form that communicates my skill set.”

“Just tell me—”

“It's short when delivered correctly.”

Somewhere across the water, beside the Sins' latest camp, Kaze was discussing the same man without receiving any of this as a telepathic invitation.

“Brian could have somebody actually like him,” he said, “and still fuck it up because they didn't announce it right.”

Arthur watched Chris lowering eggs into water.

“Shake gave him one,” Arthur said. “Now Shake's dead and he's left with Jack's weapon.”

“He likes an audience that needs him,” Daynah said.

Kaze nodded.

“Yeah. Simp lame.”

Chris looked up.

“He ain't here. You don't get points.”

“I wasn't playing.”

“Convenient.”

Back at the salvage yard, Brian raised one hand.

“Questions at the end.”

Starkiller stood very still.

Brian began.

I always knew since a lil B. Moo
that I would grow up
scratching turn tay-boo’s.
Five ten with the pimp game, some say that I’m a simp lame.
But like this—that’s just inaccurate. Sorry to ruin the flow, but—
I grip my dick just like how I rap, I mic fist.

Old school hip hop head.
I was dead, then came back attached to a hip, all head.
Meaning I was decapitated, but still a talking head.
They say that hip hop’s dead,
so I tell ’em Kaze killed me off-screen.
What a waist, thinking that I hip-hopped, dead.

Doctor Evil? More like Doctor Smeagol.
But anyways, back to the topic, my star killa.
I know I’m short and white as vanilla,
but I can become your apprentice,
you can be my Darth Vade-da.
And together we can gangbang the Seven Sins gang members—
like in the ass with our fucking lightsabers.
Nailed it!

T. P. P.? Yeah, I failed it, I bailed it.
Two weeks’ notice? Never mailed it.
I’m still lit, like a star being killed.
You get it because—
Anyways, it’s like this.

We can play Busta Rhymes while we break necks
like our necks got five wrists.
That’s a Busta Rhymes bar and a Theo Von bar at the same time.
You just wouldn’t get it.
Because it’s like this.

You’re from Star Wars?
Well, I’m from far, far away.
B. Moo come with hard bars like I’ve been behind bars,
dropping soap bars like I’m gay.
Now that’s just for the punchline’s sake.
I will have you know, Mister Killer Star,
that I am not a homosexual,
and that I only do business with smart smarts,
and not retards like Jar Jar.
More like ree-tar-tar.

He closed his eyes on the last syllable.

Then opened one.

Starkiller had not moved.

Brian smiled.

“Nailed it.”

A cart passed behind them. One wheel squealed. Nobody else volunteered to join the conversation.

“Well?” Brian asked.

“The ship.”

“Honest feedback first.”

“It was good.”

Brian's smile weakened.

“What was?”

“Your performance.”

“Any particular part?”

Starkiller looked at the journal.

Brian lowered it.

“Because people say good when they didn't actually listen. I'm used to it. I can do the middle again. That's where the structure—”

“The hip.”

Brian stopped.

“The head attached to the hip,” Starkiller continued. “Then the waist. You connect the body to the death.”

Brian slowly nodded.

“You caught that.”

“Yes.”

“Most people don't.”

Starkiller did not have the luxury of finding out whether that was true.

“The break in the rhythm draws attention to it,” he said.

Brian's pleased expression changed.

“So you're saying the rhythm broke.”

“You did it deliberately.”

“Exactly.”

“A choice.”

“A stylistic choice.”

“And asking me to become Vader puts the demand back on the teacher. You offer apprenticeship, then make the master prove himself.”

Brian had a moment in which he could have admitted he had not meant that.

“Exactly. That's the subtext.”

Starkiller inclined his head by an amount that would have qualified as nothing in a less desperate negotiation.

Brian leaned closer.

“And the wrist line?”

Starkiller's right hand flexed.

“You explain it.”

“It's two references. Busta Rhymes. Theo Von. Like this. Five wrists.”

“Yes.”

“Do you get the rhyme?”

“Yes.”

“Say it.”

A pause.

“Like this. Five wrists.”

Brian beamed.

“There it is. It sounds basic when somebody else does it.”

I would like to pause here and acknowledge the Sith's composure. You think hate powers the dark side? He was standing in front of a renewable energy source.

Starkiller looked toward the yard entrance.

Brian mistook it for a moment of professional reflection.

“The prison section too,” Brian said. “Bars. Bars. Soap bars. It's all linked.”

“I understood.”

“You don't seem like you enjoyed it.”

“The construction is effective.”

Brian opened his journal again.

“I might've rushed it.”

“No.”

“If I take it from far, far away—”

“You made yourself clear.”

Brian held the page open.

“Clear isn't necessarily memorable.”

“I will remember it.”

The tiny man waited.

Starkiller looked back down.

“Your explanations are part of the performance.”

Brian considered that with deep seriousness.

“That's what I've been saying. People try to separate them.”

“Don't.”

“I shouldn't?”

“No.”

There. A man who could move objects without touching them had found the one thing he could not get out of his way.

Brian tucked the saber beneath his arm.

“So training. You think it's possible.”

“We can discuss what you need after I have the transport information.”

“That's a very encouraging way of putting it.”

“Information.”

“Absolutely.”

Brian held out the pencil.

“Could you sign?”

Starkiller looked at it.

“My journal. Under the lyrics.”

For the first time, Brian seemed shy.

It lasted until the pencil changed hands.

“Not across the lines. I may record those.”

Starkiller wrote his name in the space below the last bar.

Brian read it.

“And a little feedback.”

“You have the feedback.”

“In writing. So I can refer to it during development.”

Starkiller added one word.

Unforgettable.

Brian stared.

“In what way?”

Starkiller slowly looked up.

“Because that could be negative. People say things are unforgettable after an accident. I'm not saying you mean it that way. Just for accuracy.”

The pencil went back down.

I loved the wordplay.

Brian let out the breath he had been holding.

“That's perfect. Could you address it to B. Moo?”

A longer silence.

“So it's personalized.”

Starkiller wrote the name.

Brian read the whole inscription twice, angled the page toward the light and waved it gently to dry.

Then he finally gave the lead.

Chris owned a blue Subaru that changed into an X-wing. It was the same vehicle, stored through a little ball, not sitting unattended in a hangar. At the last actual meeting, Chris and Billy had been at the coastal export depot beside the ropewalk. Brian had heard Arthur say they intended to head inland after selling the remaining cargo. The buyer under the blue awning could identify the group. Brian described the inlet and the route from the northern landing as he had traveled it.

He did not have new coordinates.

He did have names, directions and a visible place to start.

Starkiller asked two practical questions.

Brian answered them.

“And obviously, if you're going there as my mentor, we can discuss how to approach—”

The Force hit him before he finished approach.

His feet left the ground. His bag snapped against his back. The journal flew open.

Brian grabbed for it.

Not the yard rail.

Not the water container.

The signature.

He folded both arms around the book as he shot through the open gate and struck the first dune shoulder-first.

Sand burst over him.

The water container split against a buried stone.

Starkiller lowered his hand.

The squealing cart wheel passed him again.

He turned toward the trader who had brought it.

“The northern landing.”

The man pointed.

Starkiller walked that way.

Behind the dune, Brian spat sand out of his mouth, checked the inscription and found it intact.

He shut the journal.

“Strong initial assessment.”

On the coast, Chris set the first boiled egg behind a rock.

Meatwad was inside Billy, waiting to be let out for the hunt. Chris had spent two silver on the eggs and convinced everyone that a search for objects smaller than a clenched fist could, for once, be an ordinary fucking activity.

Four seconds later, holy light shone through cracks in the shell.

Chris turned around.

A white ray passed across his cheek.

He watched the egg split.

“No.”

The light widened.

“No, we're closed.”

A figure rose through it.

Bare feet touched the earth. Robes settled. Jesus looked around the camp.

Chris put the basket down.

“I can't fucking enjoy anything, can I? I just wanna be an ordinary moose knuckle menace, man. I boil something, I hide it. That's the whole job.”

Kaze sat up.

“Oh, shit.”

Arthur set his cup down.

Daynah put a hand on Mahnah's collar before the dog could investigate the steaming shell.

From Chris's headgear, Billy said, “Cheap entrance.”

Jesus looked at the mask.

Then at Chris.

“Billy?”

Chris smiled despite himself.

“Oh, he knows you.”

“There are men at fairs,” Billy said, “who learn a name before they approach.”

“You ate him.”

“I ate an impersonator.”

“The priest checked his stuff.”

“And clergy have never made a mistake.”

Jesus watched the little speaker.

“You thought I was pretending.”

“I continue to think so.”

Chris laughed.

“Listen to him. He knows damn well.”

Billy's voice grew warmer.

“Christopher, would you mind asking our guest to go scam somebody else's household?”

“Come out and tell him yourself.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“I have responsibilities.”

Inside, Meatwad stood beside Billy's full-sized interior self with an empty bowl, waiting to be released for Easter.

Billy gently moved him away from the exit route.

“Extensive responsibilities.”

Chris folded his arms.

“You told us you owed Jesus an apology. Here he is.”

“A convenient coincidence for a criminal.”

“You're a criminal.”

“Then I recognize the trade.”

Jesus lowered himself onto the rock beside the broken shell.

“You can talk to me.”

“I am,” Billy said. “Through suitable protective equipment.”

Chris shook his head.

“Fuck it. Sorry about my roommate. You need anything? Help getting somewhere? Something to wear on your feet?”

Jesus looked relieved.

“My cross. And the crown.”

Chris stopped.

Kaze leaned forward.

There it was. The exact moment religious tolerance ran into the display cabinet.

Jesus continued.

“You kept them.”

Chris picked up the basket.

“According to who?”

“I remember them.”

“Everybody knows what a cross looks like.”

“The ones Billy swallowed with me.”

Chris looked at Arthur.

Arthur lifted both eyebrows.

“Sounds like he knows.”

“Or somebody told him.”

Billy's voice returned at once.

“Research.”

Chris nodded.

“Targeted.”

“I asked for my things,” Jesus said.

“Your alleged things.”

Jesus looked toward the mask again.

“You said the priest checked them.”

Chris's face changed.

“Why you listening so carefully?”

“You're talking to me.”

“You hear how he talks? Everything's a fucking riddle with this guy. I ask where you're from, I'm from the light. I ask whose cross, I am the receipt.”

“I didn't say either of those.”

“That's how it starts.”

Kaze held his stomach.

“Let him see the crown, man.”

“Why?”

“So he can identify it.”

“That is exactly how theft happens. You bring the thing out to establish what it is, now it's out. Step one accomplished.”

Arthur nodded.

“Dangerous. Man gets to looking at his own belongings, who knows where it'll end.”

Jesus held up his empty hands.

“I won't take them from you.”

Chris immediately looked at the hands.

“The holes aren't proof.”

Kaze went still for a second.

Then his laugh came back worse.

“You were gonna use the fucking holes?”

“I was eliminating a line of argument before it wastes our time.”

Billy murmured through the headgear.

“Experienced operators anticipate verification.”

Chris pointed at the mask.

“Thank you.”

He did not look at Kaze, because Kaze was close to falling off the log.

“Christopher,” Billy said, with genuine satisfaction, “I am so pleased you've remained open-minded.”

Kaze started laughing.

“You was just telling him to apologize.”

Chris pointed at Jesus.

“Before he started casing my fucking house.”

Jesus looked at the basket.

“I came from the egg.”

“Exactly. No appointment. Just straight into the yard. And first thing is where's my cross, where's my crown. You don't ask if I'm all right after a fucking man hatches out of my groceries.”

“You asked what I needed.”

“A ride. A drink of water. Not the museum.”

Arthur turned his cup in his hands.

“Borrowing your own cross. Bold sort of scam.”

Chris looked at him.

“You helping?”

“Trying to understand the crime.”

Billy took the opportunity.

“Do you still claim that your mother is still virgin? Or do you want to admit that she was a dirty whore! She cheated on your father, with the neighbor! Love thy neighbor? She went out there and pulled a Judas, way before Judas.”

Jesus stared at the speaker.

“That's my mother.”

“I've identified the subject correctly.”

“You don't know her.”

“I know she had you.”

Chris held up one hand.

“Billy. Jesus Christ.”

“Yes?” Jesus said.

Billy pounced.

“There. Why did you yell your own name when I swallowed you, if you're actually Jesus?”

“I was frightened.”

“Of what?”

“You.”

Billy paused.

“Well, that part stands up.”

Chris gave the mask a sharp look.

Billy recovered.

“A convincing impersonator would be frightened too.”

“You swallowed the cross with me,” Jesus said.

“Lengthwise,” Billy corrected.

Silence.

Kaze lowered his face into both hands.

Chris looked up at his own headgear as though he could glare through the wiring.

Billy continued.

“A detail the fraud could have acquired from a witness.”

“You were the witness,” Arthur said.

“And I remain unconvinced.”

Jesus closed his eyes.

I have seen a man negotiate with the police while wearing the stolen trousers. I have never seen the trousers ask for proof they had legs.

Chris put the basket under his arm.

“Look. You want an apology for what happened? Talk to him. I just wanted to do Easter for Meatwad.”

“Then do it,” Jesus said.

“With you standing there? He finds one of these and now I gotta explain whether he's meant to put it in the bowl or baptize the fucking thing.”

“I don't need to stay.”

“You need my cross.”

“My cross.”

“See? Keeps coming back to the valuables.”

Jesus stood.

“I didn't ask you to collect them.”

“Everybody always says I didn't ask. Nobody asks. That's the problem.”

Chris set the basket down again, harder.

“I try cereal. Normal bowl-of-cereal behavior. A fucking Eyehole mascot turns up to kill me over breakfast. Not even the shop. The man on the box wants me dead.”

Kaze held up one finger.

“Good cereal, though.”

“That's not the point.”

“Just saying.”

“Then there's Mr. Nimbus. I got a grown man who looks like he sleeps varnished telling me he's some kind of ocean authority. I'm not running an aquarium. I'm trying to survive eating fucking cereal.”

Jesus stayed quiet.

Chris had found the whole drawer.

“Then Micah Bell. Which ought to be simple. Shoot the rat, go home. Except Bob Ross is living in him. Dutch's twin brother. I'm in a gunfight and suddenly the bullet's got a fucking art-school scholarship attached to it.”

Arthur looked down.

“You knew Bob was there,” he said.

“I know. That's why it's complicated. It isn't five normal bastards and then lunch. It's one bastard with somebody else's family tragedy riding around in his fucking meat.”

Billy made an approving sound.

“Choice phrasing.”

“Then Jack. Adult Jack. Clifford. The kid I couldn't be bothered playing as turns up grown and remembers all the shit we did. So now my game has fucking custody evidence.”

“You pushed him off,” Arthur said.

“You helped with the name.”

“I did.”

“Thank you. Shared responsibility. Look at us growing.”

Chris pointed toward the road without looking at it.

“Then Colm O'Driscoll. Except he's not Colm. He's Stephen Hawking. Don't look at me like that. I found out after. And this one”—he tapped the headgear—“went to prehistoric school with him.”

“We were acquainted.”

“You mourned the chair.”

“It was a beautiful machine.”

“You ate it.”

“Grief is individual.”

Chris spread his hands at Jesus.

“That. That's what I live with. Other people have an annoying roommate that leaves a pan in the sink. I have a Jurassic fucking youth pastor eating his class reunion.”

Daynah laughed once.

Chris kept going.

“My fish turns into Charles Manson. I go to sit down, and the decoration's got fucking opinions and wants to live in my house. Meatwad moves in. Then the milkshake and the floating fries, and one of them fucks off to France because apparently I'm the one who has to be reasonable about that.”

His voice caught on the missing milkshake.

He looked toward the submarine, then away.

“And the tree. Keke. You think you get a plant, maybe some shade. No. Family. Another place for somebody to fucking hurt us.”

Nobody interrupted that part.

Chris looked at the cracked shell beside Jesus's foot.

“So I think, eggs. That's got to be manageable. No guns. No goddamn disguise. Not somebody else's dead brother talking through a man I already hate. Boiled eggs. A little hunt.”

He pointed at Jesus.

“And then you lay this white dog shit on me? I mean, what the hell Jesus? If that's even your real name.”

Jesus looked down at the shell.

Then back up.

“It is.”

“That's exactly what you'd say.”

Billy sighed through the speaker.

“Christopher, I tried to warn you.”

Kaze fell backward laughing.

“You was on his fucking side for thirty seconds!”

“New information.”

“He asked for his shit!”

“Allegedly.”

Jesus took one step toward Chris.

Chris lifted the basket between them.

Not a weapon. A barrier made of the last surviving part of his afternoon.

Jesus stopped.

He waited until Chris lowered it.

“Can you at least let Meatwad out?”

Chris looked toward the mask.

Billy had gone quiet.

At last he said, “I suppose an egg hunt needn't suffer because a stranger's conduct has been disappointing.”

Chris inverted. Billy took the exterior, allowed Meatwad down, and yielded back to Chris with the basket.

Meatwad surveyed the scene.

He saw the cracked shell.

“You found one?”

Jesus knelt.

“I suppose I did.”

“That one's mine.”

Chris closed his eyes.

Meatwad picked up half the shell, inspected the empty interior and held it toward him.

“Can you hide it again?”

“Yeah. Sure.”

Meatwad handed it over and turned away to give him a fair chance.

Chris looked at the half shell.

Then at Jesus, who had wisely not asked again for the cross.

He tucked it behind the rock.

For several seconds, nothing happened.

Meatwad found it.

He put it in his bowl.

Chris watched until the next egg stayed an egg.

Across the desert, Brian got up with sand in his shoes, his water sinking into the dune and a glowing endorsement safe against his chest.

He looked toward the yard.

The broken container dripped once.

Brian shut his mouth on the speech he had been preparing and started walking.

A Little Feeling

Brian made it almost to the top of the dune before he tried to drink from the broken water container again.

He tipped it.

Nothing.

He shook it, as though the water might be in there refusing to participate.

A grain of sand dropped onto his tongue.

Behind him, somewhere beyond the ridges, stood a yard containing shade, people and presumably water. Brian had left it because going back would mean passing the gate Starkiller had thrown him through.

He looked at the signed journal.

“To B. Moo. I loved the wordplay.”

Then at the dune.

“Unconventional teaching style.”

Wade Wilson here. I have worked with a man whose primary communication tools were claws and a lifelong refusal to moisturize. Even I can tell the difference between tough love and being launched off the fucking property.

Brian tucked the book beneath his shirt and kept walking.

The next ridge looked lower.

It wasn't.

By the time he reached it, the glare had flattened the distance into one long white mistake. His green hair stuck against his forehead. He pulled his collar away from his neck and found no cooler air waiting underneath.

He tried to call.

What came out was a small, scraped sound.

Brian stopped pretending he had chosen this route.

He turned.

His tracks went downhill, then bent behind a dune. Beyond that, wind had brushed over the places where his feet had been.

He took three steps back.

On the fourth, his knee folded.

The journal hit the sand under him.

He pulled it beneath his chest, tried to rise and got one elbow straight before the desert tilted.

The light went out.

The doctor lifted the purse toward his own collar.

Then Baldur stopped moving.

Doctor Evil carefully lowered it.

Baldur turned.

The doctor held it out.

“Refund.”

Baldur looked at it.

“I should clarify that I am a doctor in a very different sense.”

Baldur walked toward him.

The doctor swallowed.

“Not that sort of swallowing-a-pencil, looking-in-your-ear doctor. My specialty is largely—”

Baldur took the purse.

The doctor shut his mouth.

For several seconds they stood close enough that the doctor's careful smile began to shake.

Then Baldur turned and walked out through the ruined wall.

He did not look back at the body.

The crewmen stayed where they were until his footsteps faded.

Doctor Evil waited longer.

Then he rose, brushed grit from his knees and looked at the broken shelter.

One of the crewmen came forward.

“Should we fetch someone?”

The doctor looked at Shang.

“No hurry.”

The man glanced toward the road Baldur had taken.

“And him?”

“Absolutely no hurry.”

A strip of burned cloth detached from the beam overhead.

The doctor watched it drift down.

The remaining piece of the sign now read SENSATION.

He picked up a length of broken wood and pushed the burning edge away from his shoes.

“Take that down.”

“Sir?”

“The sign.”

The crewman reached for it.

Doctor Evil stopped him.

“Actually, turn it around.”

The crewman did.

On the plain back, the doctor wrote CLOSED.

He considered it.

Then added: WE FEEL TERRIBLE.

Across the water, three mornings had passed since Brian burned the poster.

He had spent the first recovering, the second walking without dizziness and the third discovering that people were imitating him.

He came around the awning with Jar Jar's breakfast and found an adult Jawa standing on a crate.

The Jawa's knees opened.

Closed.

His hips jerked forward.

Brian stopped.

A second Jawa clapped a rhythm on the cart.

The first leaned back, made an exaggerated effort noise and nearly fell off.

The adults around the cart howled.

Brian slowly lowered the bowl.

Behind them, one of the Tusken scouts performed an even larger version, elbows out, knees bent, every movement delivered with the grave commitment of a man demonstrating how to survive a sandstorm with his groin.

Brian's mouth opened.

Closed.

He looked down at his own feet.

Then at the growing audience.

“Oh, shit.”

Jar Jar arrived beside him.

Brian put the bowl into his hands without looking.

“Oh, shit.”

“Yousa okay?”

“They're doing me.”

Jar Jar watched the scout.

Brian pointed.

“The movement. That's mine.”

The Jawa on the crate noticed him.

He made the little pumping motion again and pointed back.

The group laughed harder.

Brian's face brightened.

“They know.”

He hurried forward.

Not running. Artists did not run toward their own relevance.

He walked very quickly.

“Okay. First of all. I see you.”

Nobody understood why he had begun addressing them, but several turned.

Brian spread his hands.

“I see the love.”

The Jawa clapped twice.

Brian nodded.

“Exactly.”

Jar Jar stood at the edge of the circle holding both breakfasts.

Brian climbed onto an empty crate beside the performer.

“Now, there's context.”

The drumming stopped.

Brian pointed toward the small ring of people.

“Don't stop. Keep the energy. This is a conversation.”

The Jawa resumed, uncertainly.

Brian began moving his shoulders against the rhythm.

“You're seeing one element of an overall approach. I come from music. Performance. Different disciplines. The body is another instrument.”

He made a small hip movement.

The circle erupted.

Brian grinned.

“Right?”

He did it again.

The Jawa beside him copied the motion, then lifted the back of his robe and flashed his bare backside.

The laugh doubled.

Brian's smile stiffened.

“That's not necessarily part of the core.”

The Jawa looked back at him.

Brian pointed at his own face.

“Focus here.”

The Tusken scout turned around and briefly produced a competing pair of cheeks.

Brian looked from one to the other.

“Okay, now we're losing the language.”

Jar Jar set the bowls down.

“Maybe themsa just having fun.”

“They can have fun. I'm not anti-fun. I just don't want the message reduced to somebody's fucking ass.”

The Jawa slapped the crate.

The rhythm returned.

Brian started speaking over it, then stopped.

His head tilted.

He listened.

The beat was lopsided because the cart's loose iron handle rattled after the strike. Brian held the handle still, tested the wood with two fingers and found a cleaner sound near the corner.

He tapped.

The Jawa answered.

Brian tapped again, leaving space.

The answer landed in it.

For several moments the two of them built something together. No common language required. Wood, metal, hands and the little delay between one person's sound and another's.

The Tusken shifted his steps to match.

A few watchers joined in.

Brian laughed.

Not the presentation laugh. The surprised one.

Jar Jar smiled over the breakfast bowls.

Then Brian pointed to himself.

“B. Moo.”

He tapped the beat again.

“B. Moo.”

The Jawa copied the sound badly.

Brian stopped playing to correct him.

“No. B. Moo. Like the letter, then—”

The rhythm fell apart.

He pointed again.

“Me.”

The Jawa pointed too.

Then thrust his hips.

Everybody laughed.

Brian's face tightened.

“There's more to it.”

The Jawa had already started the beat again.

Brian put a hand over the striking palm.

“No. Hold on.”

The Jawa pulled away.

Brian addressed the circle.

“I'm trying to give you access to the actual artist.”

The Tusken scout sat down.

Somebody else went back to work.

Brian watched them leave.

“That's fine. People have responsibilities. I respect that.”

He waited.

Neither came back.

“So what we're going to do is take it from the top.”

Jabba's voice rolled across the yard.

The drumming stopped.

A cart stood crooked near the awning, its way blocked by the gathering. The Hutt pointed at the gap where it needed to pass.

The adults moved.

Brian remained on his crate.

“I can wrap this up.”

Jabba spoke again, sharper.

Brian climbed down.

The cart rolled through.

Jabba watched him.

Brian saw the opportunity and took it by the throat.

“You see the turnout.”

The Hutt's eyelids lowered.

“People.”

“Exactly. An audience.”

“Move them.”

“I can do more than move them. That's what I'm saying. You've got something here. They're already responding. With the right presentation—”

Jabba pointed toward the water jars.

Brian stopped.

“No.”

The Hutt waited.

“I'm not carrying cups professionally. We discussed this.”

Jar Jar hurried over and took Brian gently by the elbow.

“Breakfast.”

“In a minute.”

“Now.”

Brian looked up.

Jar Jar wasn't smiling.

Behind them, the Jawa had begun to imitate Brian's hand gestures.

The little speech.

The pointing.

The way he'd stopped the music to announce himself.

A Tusken copied Brian's offended turn toward Jabba.

The others laughed again.

Brian watched.

His face lost some of its color.

Then he pointed triumphantly.

“There. Range. They've moved into character work.”

Jar Jar led him away before he could offer notes.

Under the awning, the food had gone cold.

Brian sat.

For a while he ate without speaking.

Then he put down the spoon.

“It's early.”

Jar Jar looked at him.

“An audience doesn't necessarily understand the whole vision immediately.”

Jar Jar took a bite.

Brian leaned forward.

“You know I'm more than that.”

“Mesa know yousa hungry.”

“I'm being serious.”

“So am mesa.”

Brian looked at the bowl.

He picked up the spoon again.

At noon, Jar Jar tied his bag shut.

The northbound travelers were ready to leave the water stop. He had found space with them for the walk toward the landing and had enough supplies to make it without depending on Jabba.

Brian packed quickly.

Saber wrapped. Journal inside the bag. Three coins.

He checked the place where the poster had been.

His hand stayed there a moment.

Then he closed the flap.

Outside, the imitation had survived his attempt to organize it.

An adult Jawa was spinning a strip of cloth overhead while a Tusken performed the knee movement with such appalling concentration that another scout had to sit down laughing.

Brian stood in the doorway.

He raised one hand.

The Jawa waved the cloth at him.

Brian lowered his hand to his heart.

“Love you too.”

Jar Jar waited beside the road.

Brian joined him.

“You ready?” Jar Jar asked.

“Yeah.”

They started walking.

Behind them, somebody made Brian's little effort grunt.

The camp broke into laughter.

Brian kept his eyes forward.

After a while, he pulled out the journal while walking and found a blank space.

Jar Jar glanced down.

“What yousa writing?”

“Just documenting the response. You forget details otherwise.”

He wrote: First international following.

Beneath it: Movement spreading organically.

The torn note slipped out from between the pages.

Good words. We should make something.

Brian caught it before it reached the road.

Jar Jar slowed.

“Friend?”

Brian stared at Shake's handwriting.

The camp noise faded behind them.

“Someone I worked with.”

“Yousa miss him?”

Brian folded the note and put it back.

“We had creative differences.”

Jar Jar waited for more.

Brian shut the book.

Then, very softly, he tried the opening cadence Shake had shown him.

The first two words landed.

This time, the pause was right.

Brian tried it again.

Jar Jar smiled.

“Yousa make that?”

Brian looked up at him.

“Yeah.”

He tucked the journal away.

“All me.”

# A Little Feeling64–65 — full-text editorial review
Change ID: S7NS_E64_E65_SAME_SPAN_REVIEW_20261023.
Scope: review the exact64–65 sent, not66–67. NO PLAY. Original manuscript preserved.
Manuscript: continuity/features/E64_E65/S3_E64_E65_A_Little_Feeling_R8_20261024.txt
SHA256: 8f84e290c0f6911c11fa0f780ca12b71f26afc42be228ad8684b57e799d09c20
Evidence: full40587-character manuscript reread in contiguous0–20500/end chunks this review; Drive text matches Git. Earlier full chat also present. No machine-export chat byte comparison claimed.
Authority: latest direct Kaze correction, R9 standard, R6 raw/TTS lyrics and protected premises, sole Scene Decision Doctrine.
Status: actual original delivered through65 remains DELIVERED_PROVISIONAL, author acceptance NOT_ASSERTED. Replacement64–65 NOT_WRITTEN by this review. Playback held. Next new episode66 is separate from current revision target64–65.

## Editorial findings — AI execution, not defects in Kaze's raw material
1. Filler changed costume. Multiple bowl/water exchanges, cup-carrying status dispute, mat placement and reassurance repeat Brian wanting respect and JarJar being kind. Necessary recovery and one meaningful kindness are useful; the accumulation delays the selected encounters and poster payoff. Replace weaker repeated business with comic action from established participants; do not pad elapsed recovery.
2. The signed rap is largely an inert prop. Its compliment appears at the opening and the JarJar insult is hidden, but Brian never meaningfully performs it for Jabba/JarJar. Latest instruction now explicitly requires recurrence to established characters in the64–65 revision. This was a later author addition, not falsely described as an earlier breached instruction. Original text/meaning stays; listener reaction should change something.
3. JarJar is too narrowly a patient caregiver. Cups, meals, reassurance and restrained advice dominate. Compassion is appropriate but does not exhaust his distinct personality, clumsiness, resourcefulness, diplomacy, independent homeward purpose or potential comic friction. Do not make him cruel merely to increase intensity.
4. Jabba is thinly used. His short commands, laughter, modest bargain and cup order often function like a generic intimidating trader. Existing source limits do not require a palace or extra henchmen; sharper leverage, appetite, self-interest and independent choices must make this Jabba encounter worth its cast.
5. Brian repeatedly uses the same respectable managerial register: “Controlled conditions,” “Going forward,” “establish the basis,” “Sustainability,” “Strong route.” Expertise/status language belongs in his source, but the concentration flattens his DJ associations, compulsive rhyme/explanation, grandiose self-review, ugly reactions and abrupt plain sincerity. Protect deliberate awkwardness in Kaze's authored bars.
6. The imitation payoff risks changing the original mechanism. Initial delight is right, but loss of color and instant “character work” reframing read as embarrassment management. Kaze selected delusional belief in a real fanbase. Keep the distinction between genuine self-belief and knowing pretense clear. The collective rhythmic collaboration is viable contrast, but the long branding correction sequence makes the gag administrative and returns attention to unnamed performers.
7. Wade's voice is intermittent; much of the prose is neutral close-third narration with clipped reaction fragments. The poster line explaining “a two-foot man mediating a breakup...” describes the joke just before Kaze's payoff. Other lines explain implications already visible. More purposeful, personally invested Wade narration and fewer explanations are needed; no compulsory interruption of protected performances or emotional scenes.
8. Formulaic sentence/turn rhythm persists. Claim, mild correction, pause, look, short defensive reply, narrator gloss repeats across food, cup, crowd and sales dialogue. Numerous isolated reaction fragments manufacture pauses without adding escalating meaning. Vary interruption, sustained voice, physical consequence and silence; do not remove all pauses.
9. Shang/Baldur has a strong actual collision but repetitive middle. Warming liquid, smoking instrument, first skull, larger skull repeatedly deliver “nothing.” Physical escalation is real, but the bargain/exploitation does not change enough between attempts. Condense duplicate testing and strengthen distinct choices. Baldur's honest hope, offered risk and subsequent cruelty can stand. The eventual death was author-selected in principle; superior power winning decisively is not itself a defect, and no invented spell must prolong it.
10. Evil often supplies mild sitcom buttons—“Usually staffing,” “loading shed with aspirations,” “WE FEEL TERRIBLE”—and repeatedly ducks. A few lines can work, but they cannot carry his full specific vanity, ceremony, opportunism and menace or the desired comic intensity. Preserve the useful refund/body-purse action while rebuilding weaker interjections.
11. Some action/object staging needs tightening. After the remaining table slab shatters, Shang places the “broken table” between them and Baldur hits “the table” aside; identify actual remaining chunks rather than a visually re-formed table. The cloth-fronted sign's burns, fall and later reversal need a single legible physical state. These are clarity problems, not proof of a new canon power.
12. Runtime remains below the standing target:3182 and3560 words, about21.2/23.7 minutes at assumed150wpm, not measured audio. There is still removable slack. Replace weak material with developed consequential comedy; do not add procedure to reach duration.

## Preserve while repairing
- Actual mid-thrust awakening before Jabba/JarJar; brief discoverers remain unnamed adults.
- Small real saber success and Brian retaining the single stolen hilt, without Force/training.
- The incompatible JarJar insult and desired signature; preserve original raw lyrics and the authored awkward explanation mechanisms.
- Kaze's complete poster-breakup words and intended silence/kiss/fire/knees/scream/tears; cut competing explanatory scaffolding, not the authored payoff.
- Baldur's sensation deprivation and no magical cure; “I could get fucking angry before I paid you” is a useful selected reversal; his realization that Shang can feel the injury is a strong dark turn.
- Ending where Brian claims Shake's practiced cadence as “All me” preserves his ugly self-justification without a moral lecture.
These strengths are editorial judgments, not blanket author acceptance.

## Scope correction for next work
Apply R9 to REVISED64–65 first. Existing Jabba/JarJar are available listeners; do not import Mimir, Evil or Sins to the water stop without actual travel/access. Earlier R9 four scene options remain PROPOSED and conditional, not an approved audience parade.
No replacement manuscript drafted or sent by this review. Preserve original delivered events/version until a specific same-span replacement is actually written and authorized for release.

## Original writing and source comparison — 2026-10-23

Change ID: S7NS_E64_E65_SOURCE_COMEDY_FIDELITY_20261023.
Kaze now explicitly requires the comedy of his original sources to strongly influence ALL kinds of scenes across TPP, Brian and his new partners, and the Sins. This extends the existing R9 standard; it is not a request for an isolated Chris imitation or another cast of invented spectators. The current requested research supports revised64–65; NO PLAY.

### Actual coverage and authorship

Read completely in this review: the five dedicated duel source owners (Eyehole Man, Mr Nimbus, Micah, adult Jack Marston and Colm/Hawking); the full post-five-duels Charles/Hawking owner; the five corresponding older duel manuscripts and their domestic aftermath; all five confirmed Billy Specials; the Billy/Jesus scene owner; Daniel's full situational-joke owner. The R6 raw/revised Brian rap and protected scene notes were also read in full and retained.

The preserved, explicitly verbatim raw chef-origin monologue was read completely within the much larger IDC source. It is direct Kaze wording. The entire252972-character IDC container was NOT read; only its relevant opening material, including that complete protected passage. Several large backstory/arc/research owners were partly read or searched; inventorying532 logical owners is not a claim to have read them all. The older duel and Billy manuscripts contain AI adaptations of Kaze's premises: their full prose is not relabeled as Kaze's raw writing. Approved concepts and exact supplied lines remain distinguishable from AI expansion.

The old Micah manuscript itself ends with an original-delivery cutoff. No missing ending was recovered or invented. Older branches' cast/inventory events are references for comic construction, not a reset of current Season3 canon. IDC is a separate project reference; its physical Chris canon and completed revenge are not transplanted into S7NS.

### What the sources actually teach, and what64–65 missed

| Source | Specific construction worth carrying forward | Failure in my64–65 expansion |
|---|---|---|
| Eyehole Man duel | An appallingly small cereal grievance produces an actual dangerous confrontation. The ridiculous reason drives choices and consequences. | Too much comic language around cups and status; too little new consequence from the characters' obsessions. |
| Mr Nimbus duel | Sexualized regal self-importance, real police control, Chris's failed response and the committed Moose Knuckle escalation affect the fight. Losing the last word matters to the next action. | Mild claim/correction exchanges keep resetting instead of producing a stranger, harder situation. |
| Micah/Bob duel | The shared body makes hatred of Micah inseparable from harming gentle Bob. The dying “happy accident” association lands inside an actual betrayal. | I too often explain what a feeling means or soften a contradiction into routine reassurance. Intensity can include real hurt without an immediate gag to cancel it. |
| Jack duel | Cruel behavior from the player returns through a person with memory, grievance and agency. The ugly humor is personal and earned by that history. | Generic defensive branding could be spoken by too many characters; Brian's actual stolen work and crimes should make his specific self-praise worse. |
| Colm/Hawking chain | Assumed identity turns into Hawking, an apocalyptic claim becomes a grotesque failure, and the aftermath keeps changing the meaning of the apparent reveal. Billy's attachment and consumption make the escalation personal. | Repeated treatment attempts mostly restate “nothing,” rather than changing the bargain, interpretation or choice between attempts. Preserve actual mechanics and the selected fatal turn. |
| Charles aftermath | A trophy becomes a household participant. Chris's possessiveness, self-serving explanations and the intruder's own behavior create continuing friction. | My added caretaking often services Brian without giving Jar Jar an equally specific competing purpose. |
| Raw chef-origin monologue | A childhood skim-milk grievance grows through mock technical authority, bodily catastrophe, words becoming impossible actions, defensive interruptions and an abrupt return to shift work. The associations remain attached to the speaker's grievance while changing scale and function. | I supplied milder connective prose with occasional profanity. “More swearing” alone would leave the same weak construction. |
| Five Billy Specials | Grand grotesque events coexist with hospitality, vanity, competition, affection, song and grief. A ludicrous action can be taken with total emotional commitment. | Treating “humor is core” as a quip frequency would flatten the contrast that makes the outrageous turns work. The poster breakup must be performed, not diagnosed by Wade. |
| Raw Brian rap | Rhymes chain through hip/head/waist/death and bars/prison/soap; he derails himself to defend status, explain meaning and congratulate himself. The interruptions are authored comic behavior. | My Brian overuses managerial phrases and the signed journal is mostly carried, rather than actively making an available relationship worse. |
| Daniel joke owner | A recognized setup can become literal action using real available abilities; explanation, competitive response, interruption and failure can all change the bit. | Identical three-person setup/comeback rotations make speakers wait for jokes instead of act. This reference grants no new power or return for the departed Daniel. |

These are editorial comparisons, not declarations that every older AI paragraph is strong. The old adaptations also contain padding and overexplanation. Learn from Kaze's initiating ideas, exact performances, motives and reversals; do not import the old padding as his style.

### Creative application across the requested groups and scene types

For TPP, generate comedy through their different ambitions, competence, cruelty and status needs. Dr. Evil's attempt at ceremony, Dutch's sincere grandiosity and current painted worldview, Clifford's danger and personal fixation, and the others' own wants must change what happens. The criminal operation can work; a character's unnecessary next decision may make it ridiculous. No replacement cargo bureaucracy, new named subordinate or compulsory failed plan.

For Brian and the available partners, his autograph, offensive lyrics, actual technical skill, audience fantasy, jealousy and dependence provide material for bargaining, performance, conflict, travel and genuine attachment. Jar Jar can be compassionate while curious, indignant, physically disruptive or occupied with his own goal. Jabba can find Brian useful or entertaining without endorsing his talent. The adult imitation is genuinely occurring; Brian genuinely misreads it as fandom. Preserve the authored clothing/ass gag. Existing people can ignore, challenge or exploit his performance according to what they actually understand.

For the Sins and BELLY, use the established household, actual relationships, GGA opportunities, hoarding, incompatible priorities and chosen wrongdoing. The author does not need to supply each new joke. Make new comic action from the complete current owners; do not give everyone Chris's voice, have everybody act like Arthur, force a Sins cutaway into64–65, or make every victim secretly worse.

Apply the same creative ambition to action, attempted scams, ordinary conversation, travel, household friction, arguments, horror, performance, failure, success and quiet aftermath. Different scenes can use different means: a sustained rant, terse threat, escalating practical mistake, competitive lie, physical behavior, obscene comparison, badly timed honesty or unbroken silence before a payoff. These are available forms, not a rotating checklist or a mandated number per episode. Preserve the project's standing character-specific exceptions, including Daniel's always-situational-joking direction if he is actually present.

The strongest common requirement is that the joke affects the situation: what a person wants, chooses, misunderstands, reveals, destroys, owns or must now deal with. Absurdity is not optional ornament around AI filler. The AI is responsible for generating substantial fresh comedy at the demonstrated intensity while preserving distinct speech, physical facts and author-selected raw material.

PRESERVED RESEARCH, VOICE AND EVIDENCE LIMITS
Lord Starkiller — actual dark-side Sith Stalker

**Retained identity:** the dark-side alternate continuation of The Force Unleashed, not the sequel's clone. Sith Stalker armor and unstable black sabers are locked; the saber configuration is a user adaptation.

**Evidence examined:** the LucasArts Ultimate Sith Edition announcement preserved by TheForce.Net, distinguishing its Infinities continuation and Tatooine/Hoth missions; the dark-ending dialogue transcription; and Sam Witwer's official retrospective interview. PlayStation's DLC release descriptions corroborate the alternate-continuation premise, not all mission dialogue. [C17–C20]

This is a damaged, reconstructed instrument of the Emperor, not simply heroic Galen wearing an alternate costume. The DLC premise is distinct from both the main heroic ending and The Force Unleashed II. Promotional superlatives are not a measured power hierarchy.

**New scene distinction:** in the transcribed dark ending, killing Vader does not lead to secure promotion. The apprentice turns on the Emperor, loses, and wakes reconstructed into an explicitly disposable servant. That origin should not be written as cheerful, freely chosen devotion. His account of playing opposite Vader supports fear beneath aggression. Neither the interview nor gameplay marketing establishes unlimited Force power, a particular respirator dependency or the exact voice processing of the Sith Stalker. [C18]

**Writing application:** coercion, dependence and the possibility of autonomy matter more than visual menace alone. Elsewhere does not magically remove his history or dictate allegiance to Noxus.

Avoid one surreal image after another with no causal connection. A thought can develop, fail, get abandoned or become heavy rather than funny. Do not manufacture a mandatory weird-line/challenge/comeback loop.

Counter-play matters. A friend may improve the premise; Chris can enjoy the understanding. Someone may ignore it and act; Chris follows the changed situation. Someone may expose an exaggeration; Chris can falter, qualify or concede. He does not require a winning comeback. Under fear or grief his imagery may become melancholy; at intense sincerity it can disappear into short, plain language.

Claims about bizarre hometown acquaintances, childhood events or invented scenarios remain Chris’s claims. They do not update his canonical biography, install a new NPC or prove a real remembered event. The same principle applies when Billy disputes him. Original material should arise from his own current interests and relationships, not copied Theo Von stories or catchphrases.

His exact current save location/mission is unknown until shown. Kaze knows the game; Arthur has his own autonomy and is not a summoned commentator on demand.

Looting has real opportunity cost. Chris can be vindicated by something useful, be wrong about its value, resent being rushed or concede after damage. A professional kitchen’s exacting organization can coexist with broader hoarding. Arthur’s courteous bait and Daniel’s performance can draw him in; he may expose their own participation. He has not acquired an invented concert history. His preference does not change Billy’s musical influences. See the Billy source for mutual material and the preserved research dossier for eight original possibilities.

Keep chef judgment, hunting/fishing/butchery where ecology supports it, gun knowledge, fabrication, humor and actual bodily needs available. No new project or completed upgrade is invented to demonstrate competence. His standing project priorities and earned equipment remain with the full owner.

Chris and Billy are two independent people sharing one exterior-body arrangement. Chris can choose/request exterior control, accept it, refuse it or act fully inside. Neither always owns the outside. The other is full-size in persistent BELLY. Use Chris_Billy_BELLY_Source.txt for inversion, routing, the drawing, live Monitor 2 audio and outward banjo speech. 1. Chris's five genuinely different violent confrontations: Eyehole Man (dead); Mr. Nimbus (dead); Micah Bell (dead along with co-conscious Bob Ross); Jack Marston (dead); and apparent Colm O'Driscoll revealed only after lethal injury to be Stephen Hawking (dead). 2. Bob Ross is DUTCH VAN DER LINDE'S TWIN BROTHER in this story. Bob had died once already; a voodoo rite brought Bob's consciousness back into the living body of Micah Bell, with two independent consciousnesses sharing one body. Dutch knew and tolerated this tragic arrangement because it kept his twin brother with him. Chris recognized Bob's voice in the encounter and knew Bob was present before his fatal final shot at Micah. Micah reached for a second gun; Chris chose to fire. The choice killed both Micah and Bob. Bob's actual last words were accusatory, not a comforting happy-accident reassurance. The adult Jack is 19, from his post-1914 history, with recollections of how he was treated through RDR2 by Arthur and the controlling player's voice. The history includes tattooed/scarred 'Clifford' letters, cruel treatment, a killed red dog he loved, repeated cliff incidents, unmet hopes of being taken fishing, and the moment Chris shut the game off when control passed to young Jack. This was DELIBERATE, explicitly acknowledged by Chris afterward, not a slip or accident. Jack dies from the fall. Billy retrieves/swallow-routes the corpse away from digestive acid and Chris places Jack's single body in an already existing preservation vat; no revival. Chris separately collects Jack's possessions, Arthur takes his horse, Frank helps ensure wages are identified/distributed, and the disputed reserve is not a clean unlimited windfall. Dutch confronts Chris and Arthur over what happened. This scene also carries Dutch's fresh Bob grief.
5. Chris kills the apparently Colm opponent without knowing he is Stephen Hawking until the disguise/identity reveal AFTER the lethal injury. Billy recognizes Hawking and grieves his prehistoric friend/classmate, to Chris's bafflement. Chris didn't knowingly target Hawking by identity.
6. The cumulative cost of all five confrontations, the death of Dutch's twin Bob, the Clifford/Jack trauma, and Hawking being Billy's ancient friend are essential setup for Chris's desire for a normal RDR2 gaming break. His beloved mechanical fish sign Charles then becomes a physical Charles Manson, an intrusive interior roommate, with later warden/Pepsi/peanut-butter developments still future/unplayed at current IV.3. Eventually Meatwad enters by Billy's market food/acid-area survival with a legitimate internal route and asks EXACTLY: 'how far are you into the game?'
